author. since the abolition of the constitution and the ban on political parties in 1973, the absolute monarchy in swaziland has been in sharp contrast to developments in neighbouring south africa and mozambique. the current king, mswati iii, also retains supreme powers in the administrative, judicial and legislative fields and shows little willingness to share power. under his rule, the human rights situation and the standard of living suffered a sharp decline. the number of aids cases is among the highest in the world, and life expectancy has fallen along with it, adding thousands of orphans. we condemn today the unjust conviction and imprisonment of thulani maseko and bheki makhubu. however, they are not an isolated case and are part of a worrying trend to stifle freedom of expression and peaceful assembly and to ignore the demands of opposition parties and trade unions for a democratic rule of law. however, swaziland is bound by the cotonou agreement to respect democracy, the rule of law and human rights. the eu's policy towards swaziland should therefore not only aim at the immediate release of thulani maseko and bheki makhubu and all other political prisoners, but also at enabling the transition to a democratic state under the rule of law and a better socioeconomic situation.
in writing. ‒ europe is currently surrounded by crises and conflicts. the common security and defence policy (csdp) should therefore be the focus of our attention. the report suggests that the only way forward for the eu is strong international cooperation, particularly with the united nations, nato, the african union and the osce. however, this cooperation must also take place at the level of the member states, and incentives must be created for this. another important point from the eu's point of view is the strengthening of the european defence industry. i welcome the report and hope that a common eu strategy on security and defence policy will be adopted in due course.
in writing. ‒ the union is facing increasingly important security challenges, as shown by the many crises at the eu's borders (libya, sahel, ukraine, syria, etc.). it is therefore essential that we make more effective use of csdp tools and that they are integrated into an overall union strategy for action. in addition, member states need to coordinate their actions better on the international stage so as to speak with one voice. they also need to pool more resources to increase efficiency and reduce military spending. finally, as evidenced by recent cyber attacks in some member states, there is a need for member states to immediately strengthen their cyber defence capability to protect critical infrastructures, such as nuclear power plants, against cyber attacks.
in writing. ‒ the csdp is an important asset of the european strategy. it must assert itself as such. the current level of instability at europe's borders requires the eu and its member states to have a comprehensive, coherent and strong strategy for action to address the new security and defence challenges. i therefore supported the resolution calling on member states to use csdp tools more effectively, to improve the matching of internal and external security measures and to share resources more, in order to fight terrorism and organised crime, but also to strengthen cyber defence and to address the challenges of migration. the eu needs operational resources to assert its own strategic autonomy. it must also be able to protect critical digital infrastructures against cyber attacks. i hope that the european council on security and defence on 25 and 26 june will follow the same path.
in writing. the increasing number of conflicts at our borders represents a major challenge for the security of europe's 500 million citizens. the union does not yet have the operational, capability and industrial resources to form an integrated military force. this would enable it to respond to international crises more quickly and effectively, and also to become a major power in the defence of its strategic interests. the tradition of soft power which is dear to our union must be accompanied by a strong military component. there is no community of destiny without common defense. there can be no foreign policy without a defence policy of the union commensurate with its economic capacity. europe can no longer rely on the american strategic shield. it must develop a defence that is the armed arm of nato. i therefore fully support this report and any future initiatives towards a more integrated and coordinated common security and defence policy among all the member states.
in writing. ‒ according to jean monnet, 'europe will be made in crises and will be the sum of the solutions to these crises'. as regards europe and its common security and defence policy, there has been no shortage of crises and conflicts in recent years: in western europe (ukraine, georgia), in the south of the mediterranean (the revolutions in the arab world) and in the middle east (the civil war in syria). but the threat is not just external: the terrorist attacks in brussels, paris and copenhagen have reminded us of the urgent need to protect our people more and better. this requires a budgetary redirection to internal security missions. the budget is not the only issue. as the european parliament recalled this afternoon with the adoption of the danjean report, the lisbon treaty has provided us with the means to be able to intensify our policy: enhanced cooperation, permanent structured cooperation, financing and solidarity mechanisms. there is, however, a glaring lack of political will in some member states to make a concrete commitment to a common security and defence policy. this is the will which parliament reaffirms today.
in writing. ‒ the report i voted for underlines that at present the union does not yet have all the resources it needs to make a decisive contribution to the prevention or management of international crises and to the assertion of its autonomy and strategic interests. the report highlights the structural weaknesses of the missions and operations under the common security and defence policy, in particular the slowness and rigidity of the decision-making process. the report also calls for the creation of a pre-financing mechanism to help member states wishing to participate in operations bear the costs; while recognising that these operations are an important part of the union's overall approach and contribution to international security, it is noted that since 2009 missions have been deployed to enhance the visibility of the union's crisis response, rather than as strategic actions following extensive analysis and planning. the june european council will be devoted to defence. we'll have to follow up.
in writing. - i voted for the text. the union and its member states urgently need to adapt to these new security challenges, including by making effective use of csdp tools and by bringing them more closely into line with the union's foreign policy, humanitarian aid and development policy instruments, by coordinating national actions more closely and, where appropriate, by implementing new mechanisms for the expression of european solidarity in a pragmatic and flexible manner. the lines between external security and internal security are becoming increasingly blurred. i therefore call for better coherence between external and internal policy instruments and for more cooperation and coordination between member states, in particular in the fight against terrorism and organised crime, as well as in the areas of cybersecurity and immigration, under the aegis of the vp/hr.
in writing. ‒ every time a csdp operation is decided to be launched, the same problems arise, the debate goes on about who will provide what. this prevents the rapid deployment of csdp missions and these are often modest because member states are reluctant to provide large numbers of men and equipment. in fact, these problems are mainly due to the way the csdp is currently financed. at present, only 10% of the costs are collectively financed under the athena mechanism and about 90% of the expenditure is borne by the member states under the principle of 'paying the cost' - that is, the state which provides the equipment and the manpower also pays the bill. if we want to have real european solidarity and if we want to have an effective csdp, it is essential to consider an extension of the costs covered by the athena mechanism by including the expenses related to the deployment of csdp operations and missions.
in writing. ‒ i support the report on the financing of the common security and defence policy. the financing of european civilian and military missions must be adapted to new needs, for greater efficiency, more solidarity between member states and more commitments through concrete actions that are perceptible to citizens.
in writing. europe faces many security challenges, both within and outside the union. at a time when budgetary constraints also affect the defence sector, it is necessary to respond to these challenges in a coordinated manner in order to make the best use of the financial resources available. this optimisation can only be achieved through increased dialogue and close coordination between all the actors concerned. in the field of defence, the solution for the future is 'more europe'. if member states were to act in a more integrated manner, their collective budget, which currently stands at €190 billion, would be considerably reduced. according to the european parliament's study on the cost of non-europe 2014-2019, the potential efficiency gains from better coordination at european level on security and defence could reach 26 billion per year.
in writing. ‒ we note with concern that european states are spending less and less on defence, despite the need to increase their investments to respond adequately to new threats. and within these reduced budgets, the missions of the common security and defence policy represent only a small part. the legislative instruments at our disposal are also not sufficient to enable us to use these limited resources efficiently and cost-effectively. unfortunately, it is the european taxpayers who pay the ultimate price for this incoherent management. the economic crisis is often cited as a reason for this lack of funding. we should, however, see the crisis as a catalyst for european defence, given the potential savings that would result from in-depth cooperation between member states. in the scenario of a fully integrated european defence system, the total budget would be €62.9 billion instead of the €193 billion currently spent by the 28 states. the european union could have more influence on the international scene if it could achieve economies of scale for improved response capacity.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the multiple cuts in the defence budget require a rethinking of its funding. it is clear that despite a combined annual budget for european defence of around eur 190 billion, the member states are still unable to achieve the objectives set in helsinki in 1999 (i.e. deploying, in 60 days and for a period of at least one year, a rapid reaction force, if necessary, of the size of an army corps, i.e. a total for the land component of the order of 50 000 to 60 000 men, on the basis of the means made available by each country). i hope that the european council in june, which will be devoted to this subject, will be an opportunity to hold a thorough debate and to formulate concrete proposals for a reform of the financial arrangements for csdp missions and operations. in addition, concrete measures will be needed to strengthen the eu's defence capabilities in complementarity with nato, further consolidate the european defence agency and further support a common industrial and technological base.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the text, i share the rapporteur's view that despite a combined annual defence budget of around eur 190 billion, the member states are still not able to achieve the overall objectives of helsinki 1999.
in writing. ‒ for years, european defence budgets have been subject to significant cuts. while in 1997 member states spent on average 2.1% of their gni on defence, this figure fell to only 1.7% in 2007. since the 2008 economic crisis and the resulting austerity policies, this situation has worsened further. moreover, the cuts in defence budgets are made without consultation between member states. this lack of coordination puts the union at risk because it entails the renunciation of strategic capabilities crucial to the csdp. finally, the fall in european defence budgets is pushing european defence industries to increase their exports to third countries. as a result, the european defence industry is becoming increasingly dependent on the outside world, transferring sensitive technologies and promoting armed conflict in other parts of the world. for all these reasons, and if we want to safeguard europe's strategic independence, we must strengthen european cooperation in the field of defence and we must also make full use of the rules of the internal market and create a single defence market.
in writing. ‒ i approve the report on security and defence capabilities in europe. i believe that it is essential to work towards the creation of a genuine european single defence market based on common rules.
the commission has also adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of accidents. there is no community of destiny without common defense. there can be no foreign policy without a defence policy of the union commensurate with its economic capacity. europe needs a common security and defence policy more than ever to respond optimally to the many challenges that threaten its security. at a time when the european defence market is fragmented and some states are adopting protectionist attitudes, a coordinated response is needed. in this connection, the subsidies and compensation granted by national governments to their industries must be abolished. a unified european defence market would lead to substantial cost savings and would encourage modernisation and innovation by european companies. that is why i fully support any initiative to promote the establishment of a single european defence market.
in writing. ‒ a more influential europe needs a strong and active common security and defence policy, which in turn requires a more competitive and efficient defence and security sector. in reality, the defence industry in europe remains too fragmented, with significant state aid in several countries, leading to a difficult internal competitive situation. european companies are confronted by the large american groups, which enjoy a much larger market. at present, european countries share only a fifth of their equipment purchases and, even worse, they only share an eighth of their joint research and technology effort. in this gloomy context, where the economic crisis is also playing a part, we must make greater use of the means already in place to promote a genuine continental market and improve the competitiveness of our companies. this is how europe will achieve its strategic autonomy and how our common security and defence policy will gain credibility and visibility. this is the role our citizens expect from us, as well as our key allies in the world.

first legislative report of the legislature on agriculture. this report is the result of intensive collaboration with the rapporteurs of the political groups: mrs ribeiro for the ppe group, mrs müller for the alde group, mr nicholson for the ecr group, mr zullo for the efdd group, mr ropé for the greens/efa group and mr carthy for the gue/ngl group, to whom i am very grateful. with over 22 million the rapporteur. mr president, i would first like to thank my coordinator, mr paulo de castro, who trusted me to draw up this report, hélène cuisinier from the secretariat of the committee on agriculture and rural development, who was very thorough in her work, and maggie coulthard from my political group, and alexandra ionna leone, my assistant. i shall try to answer some questions and objections from members. first of all, i would like to welcome the commission's original proposal, which was in the direction of a restriction of products and in the direction of the objective pursued in the field of public health. in reply to mr rompuy, i would like to say that my group and i support amendment no 50 by the green group, which aims to eliminate flavour enhancers. so i can reassure him on that point. we have talked a lot about local fruits and products, which are indeed supported and favoured, as well as those from organic production. but we must also include seasonal fruit, because in a region like mine, for example, eating only local fruit in winter would be like eating only apples and pears, which would be tiresome for the children. although they are not produced in my country and do not come from the region, oranges and citrus fruits, as well as kiwis - which i will come back to later - are seasonal fruits and are useful for health, in particular because of their vitamin c content. mrs köstinger, as regards the amendment on chocolate milk, i should like to make it clear that i am not an enemy of this product - my ten-year-old son drinks it, not every day, but he does drink it - but, nevertheless, 200 ml of chocolate milk is equivalent to 20 grams of sugar, that is to say half the maximum tolerated and recommended intake for school-age children, which is far too sweet. mr flanagan and mr ashworth were talking about the responsibility of the european union. it is clear that 24 out of 28 countries are consuming too little fruit and vegetables, so if europe can help the member states to improve this aspect, why do you stubbornly refuse the help of the european union? i don't know what you mean. europe, while not having the right to interfere, has the right to have good ideas, hoping that the member states will implement them correctly. there will be no war between bananas and kiwis, it would be useless. both are useful fruits - the banana for its natural sugar content, the kiwi for its vitamin c content. i would remind you that in the outermost regions there are european bananas, which are preferred and which, if not, will be replaced by fair trade bananas, so of course we are trying to give preference to small producers. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to express one regret. food, fruit, vegetables, milk, are important, but perhaps we could have talked about other drinks. given the increase in the consumption of sodas and the proliferation of these products, perhaps we should have promoted drinking water, which can be a useful accompaniment. i hope that it will be valued in educational measures. like you, commissioner, i hope that the council, which is now rather conservative in its approach to practice, will adopt the common view of the commission and parliament to move towards a healthier diet through this programme of fruit, vegetables and milk distribution in schools.
in writing. by taking a position on this proposal today, parliament is showing that it really wants to continue with this programme. the commission had previously announced its intention to test the programme on subsidiarity, proportionality and better regulation and is considering de facto terminating it. we don't see it that way. in recent years, the member states and parliament have developed a coherent scheme to promote fruit in schools. by the way: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the member states are able to decide for themselves whether they wish to participate in the scheme, so that there is no ambiguity as regards subsidiarity. dietitians and policy makers today are racking their brains about how we can turn the diabetes epidemic around and promote healthier diets. that is why this programme must continue. consumption of fruit and vegetables is alarmingly low in the eu. in two thirds of the member states, the absolute minimum recommended by the world health organisation (of 400 g per person per day) is not even reached. we therefore hope that the council will soon make clear where it is going with this proposal and we count on the commission's readiness to continue with this programme as an 'impartial mediator'.
in writing. every year, some 30 million european schoolchildren benefit from the two eu-funded programmes, the school milk scheme and the school fruit scheme. these programmes are aimed at encouraging children to eat healthy foods and adopt healthy eating habits in response to the increasing rate of childhood obesity. in january 2014, the commission published a legislative proposal to merge these two programmes into a common legal and financial framework in order to increase their effectiveness and reduce the administrative burden on national and local actors. in december 2014, the new commission presented its work programme for 2015, which indicated that the legislative proposal on the merger of the fruit and milk programmes was suspended pending an evaluation under the cap simplification exercise. despite the commission's recommendation, i would ask you to vote today on this report so that work can continue on amending the legislative proposal. the adoption of this mandate is therefore a strong signal that parliament wishes to continue its work. i welcome that in advance.

in writing. ‒ the european parliament has this evening supported by a very large majority (458 votes in favour, 97 against) the report on the european programme to support the distribution of fruit and vegetables and milk in schools. in europe, the consumption of fruit and vegetables is falling steadily. european adolescents consume on average only 30 to 50% of the recommended daily intake of fruit and vegetables. in belgium, for example, expenditure on fruit and vegetables fell by 5.8% in 2014. the annual consumption per capita has risen from 95.8 to 82.7 kilos in ten years. yet, according to the world health organization, adequate fruit and vegetable consumption could prevent more than 1.7 million deaths each year, reduce the risk of obesity, and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. in the european union, 20 million children are overweight. so from an early age, it is important to instill good eating habits and promote healthy eating. that is why i have opposed the distribution of chocolate milk, which is decidedly too sweet, in this programme which will affect 30 million european schoolchildren.
in writing. ‒ every year, some 30 million european schoolchildren benefit from the two eu-funded programmes, the school milk scheme (launched in 1977) and the school fruit scheme (since 2009). these programs are designed to encourage children to eat healthy foods and to adopt healthy eating habits in response to the increasing rate of childhood obesity. in january 2014, the commission published a legislative proposal to merge these two programmes into a common legal and financial framework in order to increase their effectiveness and reduce the administrative burden on national and local actors. in december 2014, the new european commission presented its work programme for 2015, which indicated that the legislative proposal on the merger of the fruit and milk programmes was suspended pending an evaluation under the cap simplification exercise. in spite of the commission's recommendation, we decided, in voting on this report, to continue work to amend the legislative proposal. the adoption of this mandate is therefore a strong signal that parliament wishes to continue its work.

in writing. ‒ the merging of both programmes (milk at school and fruit and vegetables at school) is a good thing. it allows more to be done with less administration, and that benefits our children. i voted in favour of increasing the budget of the programme by eur 20 million because the european union is simply more countries than in the 1970s and 1990s when the schemes were introduced. every child in the eu deserves milk, fruit and vegetables at school. this will help to combat obesity. it is also beneficial for our farmers who are still suffering from the russian boycott of fruit, vegetables and milk products from europe.

in writing. the common agricultural policy has enabled european agriculture to survive, even in difficult regions, to develop, to produce sustainably and to make quality products available to all. when we voted for the cap reform, our aim was to make direct payments fairer and greener, to strengthen the position of farmers in the food chain, to guarantee food security, to ensure the sustainability of the agricultural sector and to make the cap more efficient and transparent. in this context, the financing regulation for the period 2014-2020 provides for the establishment of a financial reserve to respond to a potential agricultural crisis by charging a percentage of 1,39% on any direct financial aid exceeding eur 2 000. although this represents only a small part of direct payments, its usefulness could prove beneficial in the future.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the motion. in this respect, as a general rule, farmers applying for direct payments in respect of a calendar year (n) receive those payments within a certain payment deadline for the financial year (n + 1). however, member states may make late payments to farmers beyond this payment period, subject to certain deadlines. such late payments may be made in a subsequent financial year. where financial discipline is applied for a given calendar year, the adjustment rate should not apply to payments for which aid applications have been submitted in calendar years other than the calendar year for which financial discipline applies. therefore, in order to ensure equal treatment between farmers, it is appropriate to provide that the adjustment rate applies exclusively to payments for which aid applications have been submitted under the calendar year for which financial discipline applies, irrespective of the date on which the payment to farmers is made.

in writing. ‒ the level of harmonisation of intellectual property protection is comparatively low across the eu and with third countries. the wto trips agreement obliges signatory states to establish arrangements to ensure minimum standards and effective enforcement measures. this report now takes into account the conflicting economic interests of rightholders and users, as well as the increasing digitalisation which is posing new challenges to ipr protection. harmonisation involving third countries is useful and desirable for many reasons, in particular to allow new market entries, to promote creativity and innovation and to ensure international competitiveness in this field. in addition, the report takes account of the specific situation of the pharmaceutical industry and responds to the conflicts between the preservation of competitiveness and economic interests and the guarantee of access to medicines. i consider international harmonization in the field of intangible property protection and the creation of a worldwide standard of protection to be extremely useful and therefore welcome the above measures.
in writing. ‒ the most important element of the report, in my view, concerns safeguarding the circulation of generic medicines and stresses the balance between generic production and the protection of pharmaceutical research. the need to find a balance between protecting intellectual property and ensuring access to medicines for the most vulnerable people. intellectual property-intensive industries account for about 39% of overall economic activity (about €4.7 trillion per year) and approximately 26% of total employment (56 million jobs). however, since the entry into force of the agreement on trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights (trips) on 1 january 1995, only a limited number of significant ipr agreements have been concluded, even as technological and societal developments have transformed the ipr landscape. the communication identifies action to promote research and innovation, access to medicines and environmental issues as major challenges for today and tomorrow. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of intellectual property rights.
in writing. ‒ i supported this resolution because it is very clear that the union needs better tools to protect the union's intellectual property in third countries. the commercial nature of many ipr infringements and the increasing role of organised crime in these infringements constitute a serious threat to creativity and innovation. creativity and innovation are key assets of the union in the global market. we have to protect them. the resolution calls on the commission to address this extremely complex issue in order to balance the interests of rights holders, economic operators and end users.
in writing. intellectual property rights (ipr) make a strong contribution to the development of innovation and creativity. in developing countries, their protection is a key issue for their competitiveness and for their integration into world trade. i welcome the european parliament's vote to give the european union a more ambitious strategy for the protection of intellectual property rights vis-à-vis its trading partners. as the digital world is becoming increasingly important in developing countries, such a strategy will help to combat counterfeiting of trademarks and patents by operators from these countries. it is a step forward in the fight against copyright infringement, which causes serious financial losses and damages businesses and the economy of developing countries. by voting in favour of this strategy, the european parliament confirms the eu's interest in helping its partners develop a healthy and secure business environment.
in writing. ‒ intellectual property is about properly rewarding our researchers, creators and inventors for their original ideas and creations, and encouraging companies to invest in innovative solutions, services and products. it promotes innovation and creativity for the benefit of all. these are all reasons for us to continue our efforts with our international partners to improve standards for the protection of intellectual property rights. the commission is therefore right to decide to revise its strategy in this area. in addition, the lessons of the acta disaster have been learned: we must negotiate with countries that are lax on counterfeit goods, clearly separating the digital world from tangible goods. this revision is welcome, because the fight against counterfeiting is more urgent than ever and europe cannot win it alone. wider international recognition of intellectual property rights and the strengthening of the capacity of partner countries to protect these rights will lead to more innovation, and therefore more creative change and economic growth, for the benefit of the citizens of europe and the world.
in writing. ‒ the fight against infringements of intellectual property rights (trademarks, patents, copyright, geographical indications, etc.) is a priority for the competitiveness and the smooth functioning of europe. in 2013, 36 million items (worth over €760 million) were suspected of infringing intellectual property rights. that is why i supported the report that parliament voted on, which calls for better consideration of the challenges posed by the digital economy and for more efficient tools. the report calls on the commission to create a framework for the convergence of member states' and third countries' interests, with a mutual interest in establishing strong protection frameworks with effective remedies, in order to close the gaps in ipr protection. the text also encourages the commission and the member states to defend ipr better in all relevant multilateral organisations (wto, who) and to promote the integration into the wto system of international ipr agreements which are not yet part of the wto system, such as the wipo trademark law treaty and the wipo copyright treaty.

member of the commission. madam president, i would like to reiterate my thanks to the rapporteur for the enormous work he has done to produce a report of enormous complexity, as has been shown by the interest of the speakers - more than 80 speakers - and by the variety of views that have been put on the table and, therefore, i think that he has sought a balance of positions which is very commendable. i have seen in this debate, first of all, the interest shown by the subject of energy security. it is normal: a european union which imports 53% of its energy; in which six member states depend on russia as the only external supplier of gas; in which three states depend on russia for the operation and balance of their electricity grid; and taking into account the geopolitical situation we have experienced, this is a hot topic. but the approach to its solution is multifaceted, as we have seen: there are many ways to increase our energy security. the highest level of consensus i have seen in the debate is around energy efficiency policies. there is a consensus here that it's a win-win policy, it's a winning policy, it's a policy worth pursuing. and just a fact, which is that for every percentage point that we increase our energy efficiency, we reduce our gas imports by 2.6%, we manage to increase our energy security and, moreover, we achieve fundamental savings for european consumers. the second major policy on which there is basic agreement is the development of a genuine internal energy market in the electricity and gas sectors. in the electricity sector, the biggest problem has been raised by interconnections: the fact that there are still many member states that do not reach the 10% interconnection target set for 2020 or the 15% target set for 2030. and so one of the policies of the european commission is going to be to encourage interconnections, the development of smart grids and that electricity flows can be a reality in the european union. but the same is true of gas interconnections: we have not solved all our interconnections at the moment. we have to solve this: the midcat corridor in the pyrenees; we have to develop the networks in southern france to connect with the central european network; in central, eastern and southern europe we have to carry out more than 14 projects to make a real connection in the area. and so we must also have an ambitious policy of interconnecting the territory, because we saw during the recent crisis in ukraine how reversible flows and european solidarity were very important to guarantee energy security in times of crisis. and finally there is a policy, which everyone has also advocated, which is the need for diversification of sources, diversification of routes and diversification of suppliers. the commission is seeking to ensure that no country is dependent on a single supplier and can rely on at least three suppliers, which means developing interconnections; which means supporting the southern corridor to make the gas connection with azerbaijan and, in its day, with turkmenistan; and which means developing a liquefied natural gas strategy which is very important as an element of energy security and as a guarantee in times of crisis. but it also has an immediate effect: it increases competition. the development of liquefied natural gas with a strategy produces immediate effects. we have seen this in lithuania, where the construction of an automatic liquefied natural gas plant resulted in a 20% price reduction because there was competition on the market. the commission will therefore continue to support all developments, all actions within the framework of the energy union to make energy security a priority, and using all instruments. i would like to end by once again congratulating mr saudargas and the four rapporteurs from the four committees who have delivered opinions on this report for their work and for their collaboration with the commission in the development of this report.

in writing. ‒ the kyoto protocol, signed in 1997, set an internationally binding emission reduction target: to meet the commitment to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 8% below 1990 levels over the period 2008 to 2012. the eu ratified this protocol in 2002. at the doha climate conference in december 2012, the parties agreed to a further quantified emission reduction of 20% below 1990 levels for the period 2013-2020. for the european union, its member states and iceland, this means limiting their average annual greenhouse gas emissions to 80% of their base year 1990 emissions. the doha amendment is subject to acceptance by the parties to the kyoto protocol and will not enter into force until the instruments of acceptance have been received by at least three-quarters of the parties to the kyoto protocol. in its ratification decision 10400/2014, the council adopted the doha amendments to the kyoto protocol, which requires the consent of the european parliament in accordance with article 192 (1) and article 218 (6) (a) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. i welcome this resolution because it sends a clear signal to the efforts and leadership of the eu and its member states in the fight against climate change at international level.
in writing. ‒ the doha amendment introduces a second commitment period of the kyoto protocol, which began on 1 january 2013 and will end on 31 december 2020, and provides for legally binding emission reduction commitments under which the european union, its member states and iceland commit to limit their average annual greenhouse gas emissions for the period 2013-2020 to 80% of their baseline year emissions. the commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the establishment of a specific framework for the implementation of the union's climate and energy policy. it seems to me essential at this time to support an ambitious plan to combat climate change and greenhouse gas emissions. this amendment will extend the period of application of the kyoto protocol, so i can only welcome it.
in writing. by approving the draft council decision, parliament reaffirms the eu's leading role in the fight against climate change. the doha amendment to the kyoto protocol set more ambitious and legally binding emission reduction commitments for the second commitment period, which expires at the end of 2020. in the second period, a 20% reduction in greenhouse gases is sought. the eu and its member states have endorsed the joint ambition to reduce harmful greenhouse gas emissions to 80 per cent of the 1990 baseline. while the eu is making its commitment to combat climate change, it is regrettable that the major polluting countries are still lagging behind. the eu must use all its political and diplomatic means to persuade these countries to join the fight against climate change. a new international agreement to follow up the kyoto protocol is being negotiated in paris at the end of this year. the g7 leaders meeting in berlin this week have agreed to further reduce greenhouse gas emissions by phasing out fossil fuels by the end of the century.

in writing. i welcome the accession of croatia to the convention on mutual assistance in criminal matters between the member states of the european union. in a globalised world, dominated by the internationalisation of each of our lives, it is essential that optimal cooperation in criminal matters is established in europe to ensure that the fight against crime, and in particular transnational organised crime, is conducted vigorously and effectively. better judicial cooperation in criminal matters is the other face of the free movement of persons and the simplification of administrative formalities. justice must respond to this international crime this accession is in that direction and i fully support it.

in writing. ‒ the 2012 act on the conditions of accession of croatia to the european union simplified the accession of croatia to the conventions concluded by the member states on the basis of article 34 of the treaty on european union. it is no longer necessary, as in the past, to negotiate and conclude specific accession protocols (which had to be ratified by the 28 member states). article 3 (4) and (5) of the act of accession merely provides that croatia is to accede to the conventions and protocols under that act. those paragraphs provide for the council to take a decision fixing the date on which those conventions enter into force for croatia and to make all the adjustments made necessary by the accession of that new member state to those conventions. annex i to the act of accession lists the six conventions and protocols concerned in the field of justice and home affairs. the convention of 29 may 2000 on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters between the member states of the european union is included in this list. the report voted on today is therefore intended to make the adjustments required by croatia's accession to the convention.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the text. in its letter of referral, the general secretariat of the council informed the general secretariat of the parliament of a technical error affecting the presentation of the commission recommendation, related to the date of entry into force of the convention between croatia and the member states. in accordance with article 1 of the recommendation, the convention enters into force between croatia and the member states for which the convention is in force on that date on the first day of the first month following the date of adoption of the decision. article 3 of the decision states that it 'shall take effect' on the 20th day following that of its publication in the official journal of the european union. these arrangements could lead to a situation of uncertainty as to the actual date. the requirement of publication is an essential procedural requirement. without publication, an act is deemed to be non-existent by the court of justice of the european union. therefore, the decision must first be adopted and published; it shall then enter into force on the date specified therein. finally, the convention should enter into force as a result of the publication and entry into force of the decision.
in writing. ‒ following croatia's accession to the eu in 2013, the country is now also joining the convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the european communities or of the member states of the european union.
in writing. ‒ croatia is a full member of the european union and should therefore accede to the convention of 26 may 1997 drawn up on the basis of the treaty on european union, on the fight against corruption involving officials of the european communities or of the member states of the european union.
in writing. i welcome the accession of croatia to the convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the european communities or of the member states of the european union. the fight against corruption and fraud in the european institutions is a top priority for the union. corruption, especially that of public officials, must be vigorously combated in order to ensure the good governance of our union. this cooperation by croatia is a step in the right direction.
in writing. ‒ i supported this afternoon the report on the recommendation for a council decision on the accession of croatia to the convention of 26 may 1997 drawn up on the basis of article k.3 (2) (c) of the treaty on european union, on the fight against corruption involving officials of the european communities or of the member states of the european union.
in writing. ‒ the 2012 act on the conditions of accession of croatia to the european union simplified its accession to conventions concluded by member states on the basis of article 34 of the treaty on european union. it is no longer necessary, as in the past, to negotiate and conclude specific accession protocols (which had to be ratified by the 28 member states): article 3 (4) and (5) of the act of accession simply provides that croatia accedes to the conventions and protocols by virtue of that act. article 3 (4) and (5) of the act of accession provides for this purpose that the council is to take a decision fixing the date on which these conventions enter into force for croatia and to make all the adjustments made necessary by the accession of that new member state to those conventions. annex i to the act of accession lists the six conventions and protocols concerned in the field of justice and home affairs, including the convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the european communities or of the member states of the european union. the report voted on today is therefore intended to make the adjustments required by croatia's accession to the convention.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the text. this recommendation for a council decision, proposed by the commission, is intended to make the adjustments required by croatia's accession to the convention.
russia and the european union have been engaged in a worrying bidding war for years now, in fact since the expansion of nato to the east and russia's first military response in south ossetia in 2008, a dangerous bidding war, a spiral of mutual provocations, which are driving things to a head and which we have known since 1914 that could lead to a major war. none of these mutual provocations has improved, neither european farmers, nor russian farmers, nor the russian economy, nor the economies of the eu member states. it is one thing to condemn in the strongest terms russian violations of the principle of consultation, such as in crimea. the european union countries' commitment to a de facto geostrategic and economic attachment to ukraine, promising the population there money and immigration on behalf of the eu peoples, is another matter. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the context of the directive. we believe that these are the seeds of further escalation of the conflict.
in writing. ‒ i am convinced that a constructive, predictable relationship between the eu and russia is possible and in the mutual interest in the long term, but i regret that russia, because of its aggressive and divisive policies in recent weeks and months, can no longer be treated or seen as a strategic partner of the eu at this time. i therefore welcome the resolution adopted, as it calls for a critical reassessment of the eu's relations with russia.
in writing. ‒ in the current context, it seems to me essential to reach an agreement that would guarantee the end of the conflict in ukraine. russia has for some time been deliberately violating international law, the principles of democracy and the values of the rule of law. it seems inconceivable to me that the european union and russia should have a good relationship in the current conflict climate. i am convinced that a constructive relationship between the union and russia would be possible and beneficial if it did not violate the union's values and applied the minsk agreements. i therefore voted in favour of the landsbergis report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because at the moment vladimir putin's russia is trampling on the basic principles of international law by seeking to redraw european borders by force. i believe that any further cooperation with russia can only be envisaged on condition that it respects the territorial integrity and sovereignty of ukraine and that it puts an end to its military and security activities aimed at destabilising the borders of the european union. i would, however, encourage the european union to reach out to the russian authorities and civil society organisations which are willing to develop political and diplomatic relations with the union based on partnership and cooperation. finally, i believe that the latest measure, which prohibits the entry of political figures and officials of the union into russia, is a pure provocation by mr putin, who is clearly seeking to escalate tensions. i dare hope that russia will reconsider this decision.
in writing. in its report on eu-russia relations, which has lost its status as a privileged strategic partner as a result of its actions in crimea, parliament rightly expressed its outrage at the increasingly systematic intimidation and persecution of political activists, opposition politicians and human rights defenders by the russian authorities. the report also expressed dissatisfaction with russia's arbitrary measure to ban european politicians and officials from entering russia. parliament also instructed the commission to examine the external financing of european political parties, for example from russia, and to take appropriate measures. it is worrying that russia is increasingly behaving as a challenger to the international democratic community and its legal order. the european parliament nevertheless remains committed to a constructive cooperation relationship with russia, provided, however, that the russian authorities guarantee international law, universal values and the right to freedom of expression and respect the territorial sovereignty of ukraine, including crimea.
in writing. ‒ this afternoon, parliament reiterated its deep concern about russia. and for good reason, the russian leadership continues to violate international law and flout international norms: illegal annexation of crimea, violation of georgia's territorial integrity, measures of economic coercion or political destabilization against its neighbors, etc. the report is not much brighter in respect of democracy and fundamental freedoms. just yesterday, the eldest daughter of the russian opposition leader boris nemtsov, who was assassinated in february, denounced that "the russian media, on the orders of the kremlin, is creating a climate of violence and terror". and to top it all off, russia has just published a blacklist banning 89 european politicians, civil servants and military leaders from entering russian territory. russia's behaviour is further isolating it internationally. it is no longer one of the union's strategic partners. the eu and russia should have constructive relations, which would be beneficial to both sides. meps know this and will not close the door on the condition that this cooperation is based on dialogue, respect for international law and human rights.
in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of this report which calls on the european union to critically reassess its relations with russia. relations which are deeply damaged by moscow's deliberate violation of democratic principles, fundamental values and international law through its violent action and destabilisation of neighbouring countries.
in writing. - i voted yes. i am of the opinion that relations between the european union and russia must now be based on respect for international law and on a dialogue in which the european union would be prepared to resume and relaunch cooperation with the russian authorities in a number of specific areas of common interest. we stress that resumption of cooperation could be considered on condition that russia respects the territorial integrity and sovereignty of ukraine, including crimea, fully implements the minsk agreements (which include full border control by the ukrainian authorities, unconditional withdrawal of russian troops and weapons, and immediate cessation of support to rebel groups) and ceases its military and security activities aimed at destabilising the borders of the eu member states. the organization for security and cooperation in europe (osce) has proved to be a structure capable of contributing to the resolution of the crisis in a neutral manner.
in writing. ‒ the state of affairs between the eu and russia is not very good, to be honest. although i disagree with many of my colleagues on the approach to relations with russia, i voted in favour of this report because we as the eu must make a clear voice heard. i'm not so keen on the pit wars we're organizing. i strongly urge more dialogue on the ground. what is happening now has deeper causes and we must dare to discuss them.
in writing. ‒ in may 2014, the european commission published the strategy for european energy security in response to the worsening crisis in ukraine. the main objectives of the strategy for energy security include reducing energy demand, in particular by increasing energy efficiency, linking energy networks between member states and increasing domestic energy production. the creation of a european energy union and the completion of the eu's internal energy market are currently given priority. this own-initiative report by the itre committee supports the objectives set out by the commission. the urgency of a common energy supply strategy is mainly due to the eu's current fragile relationship with russia and the high degree of energy dependence on third countries the eu meets 53% of its energy needs through imports from third countries. i therefore welcome the measures taken in the strategy and call on eu actors to work together towards the completion of the eu internal energy market.
in writing. ‒ i believe that the energy security model is linked to the energy transition. the priority must be to ensure energy efficiency, promote renewable energy and encourage financial investment in domestic energy production, rather than spending large sums to import energy. developing the green technology industry is essential to create jobs.
in writing. ‒ unfortunately, the european parliament rejected this report, which was intended to increase safety and reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. the text called for action to be taken to moderate energy demand and increase local energy production while reducing carbon emissions. it is important to take further action to build a fully integrated and synchronised system, to put in place solidarity and coordination mechanisms and to ensure the proper functioning of the internal energy market. ensuring the union's energy security must be at the heart of our long-term energy strategy. it is the cornerstone of a fully open and free common energy market, which ensures compliance with environmental standards while stimulating economic competitiveness. member states would now have access to cleaner and more cost-effective resources without having to rely on suppliers from third countries which are politically and economically unreliable. it is appalling to see the rejection of this report, which i personally supported. this only increases the doubt about the ability of parliament to move forward on the issues that concern european citizens.
in writing. ‒ i regret that meps were unable to reach agreement on the fundamental issue of the european union's energy security and rejected the saudargas report, due to differences on the fracking issue. the energy issues go far beyond the problem of shale gas and require a long-term strategy for a genuine european energy policy. the alde group has a very ambitious strategy in this area, which i share: it is essential to go even further than the plan for the creation of the european energy union, presented by the commission on 25 february. it is imperative to break free from dependence on russian gas. clean and renewable energy is another objective that europe needs to invest in in order to maintain its technological lead. the present situation, with the union importing 53% of all the energy it consumes, is not sustainable. energy efficiency is essential in this strategy. upgrading residential and office buildings, modernising public transport, using smart technologies and innovating would boost growth and jobs, saving billions of euros.
in writing. ‒ i voted this afternoon in favour of this report, which aims to define a european strategy for energy security. the text provides, for example, that russia can no longer be considered a reliable partner because it explicitly challenges eu legislation, particularly in the wto, and exploits energy supplies for political purposes. the report also recalls that parliament has already called on two occasions for binding targets for climate, renewable energy and energy efficiency by 2030. i also supported amendments such as the phasing out of all environmentally harmful subsidies; the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the text with some specific positions taken through amendments. in insisting on the principle of solidarity, we should stress that energy security is a matter of collective action. member states must ensure transparency in negotiations and adopt a common position vis-à-vis foreign suppliers. as indicated in the commission communication on the short-term resilience of the european gas system, member states' supply strategies are currently unilateral and poorly coordinated. in this connection, we ask the commission to analyse possible mechanisms for joint gas purchases.
in writing. ‒ the european anti-fraud office (olaf) is supervised by a monitoring committee composed of five independent experts appointed by common accord of the european parliament, the council and the commission. this monitoring committee regularly monitors the investigations carried out by olaf in order to ensure its independence. the 2014 annual report presented today casts some doubts on the office's success stories. the figures were artificially inflated by tricks with statistics. in this context, i welcome the resolution which strongly calls on olaf to comply with the legal requirements for the initiation of an investigation and on the monitoring committee to monitor better compliance with these legal requirements.
in writing. ‒ olaf must of course comply with the legal requirements governing the opening of an investigation. the supervisory committee must be able to fulfil its role and verify compliance with these legal requirements. it is regrettable that the monitoring committee found it impossible to determine whether the priorities of olaf's investigative policy had been correctly identified and whether their application had had positive or negative consequences for the fight against fraud and corruption within the union.
in writing. ‒ the 2014 annual report of the olaf supervisory committee points to a number of dysfunctions between the supervisory committee and the director-general of olaf. these comments point to a worrying lack of transparency. i therefore strongly support the request to the commission to take the necessary measures to improve the capacity of the olaf supervisory committee to monitor the independence of the office, its investigative functions, the application of procedural safeguards and the duration of investigations. although olaf is an independent body, it must comply with the legal requirements governing its operation and its powers. in particular, the office shall provide without delay a justification for cases where it has not implemented the recommendations of the supervisory committee. the monitoring committee must be able to check regularly whether olaf is complying with the legal requirements governing its operation. this mandate must be able to be carried out freely, since it is essential to verify whether the priorities of the investigation policy have been correctly identified and whether their application has had positive or negative consequences for the fight against fraud and corruption.
in writing. ‒ in this time of economic turbulence, it is essential to ensure that european taxpayers' money is used appropriately and in accordance with the rules. in this context, the role of the european anti-fraud office is essential. in order to carry out its investigations successfully, the independence of olaf is a prerequisite. but if this principle is abused by the institution to escape democratic control, it risks upsetting the balance of power. however, for the third year in a row, the olaf supervisory committee has reported to us on the difficulties it is facing in carrying out its democratic control mission due to a lack of regulation. parliament therefore called on the commission to look into the revision of legal instruments and to find solutions to ensure that olaf is truly accountable. better control rules are possible, while respecting the principle of the body's independence. it is not just the credibility of olaf and the european institutions that is at stake, but also the credibility of our commitment to combating fraud involving european funds.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution which calls on the commission to facilitate the negotiations between the european anti-fraud office (olaf) and its monitoring committee by drawing up, by 31 december, an action plan for the modification of the working arrangements so as to enable the monitoring committee to fulfil its mandate under satisfactory conditions. parliament called on the commission to take measures to improve the capacity of the olaf supervisory committee to monitor the independence of the office.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the resolution and i share the astonishment of my colleagues. olaf is responsible for complying with the legal requirements governing the opening of an investigation. it is worth recalling that of the 423 files opened on the same day, only 8.4% of those which were closed resulted in the formulation of recommendations. the supervisory committee must monitor compliance with legal requirements seriously and regularly!

mr president, i have welcomed and supported the juncker plan from the beginning. i had and still have three reasons for doing so. the first reason is that everyone knows that the level of private investment in europe is far too low, even lower than it was before the 2008 crisis. i am convinced that the plan, by using private capital, with the contribution of the european investment bank and the guarantee given to it, by the multiplier effect which i believe it will have, will constitute the first step in the revival of private investment in europe. secondly, i am convinced that the european union needs an effective instrument to help finance investments with a high potential added value, but also with a significantly higher risk than others. finally, i am convinced that the fund's management structures, thanks to their professionalism and thus their independence from bargaining between member states, are a guarantee of success in the selection of promising projects. to innovate, you have to do something new and dare to step outside of corporatism. that's the challenge of the fund. i think he'll make it.

in writing. ‒ the commission is proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. the deputy prosecutor of the supreme court of greece accuses him of having, by using physical violence, illegally broken into the premises of the greek public television station ert-3 on 4 march 2010 to interrupt the noon news and read a press release. the waiver of the immunity of a member of parliament follows a very strict procedure. in the case of a member of the european parliament, immunity is covered by article 9 of the protocol on the privileges and immunities of the european union and may, as a general rule, be waived where the offence is absolutely unrelated to the performance of the duties of a member of the european parliament. the same article also states that immunity cannot be invoked in the case of flagrant misconduct and cannot prevent the european parliament from exercising its right to waive the immunity of one of its members. this derogation is usually justified either by the seriousness of the alleged facts or by the need to reach a judicial decision quickly.

in writing. rarely has a trade partnership negotiation raised such fears. the reason for this is that the proposed transatlantic treaty puts two very different markets and economic and social models in competition. we cannot accept that the harmonization of european standards is being reduced! while i am not opposed to the principle of negotiation with the united states, the mere fact that negotiators do not completely exclude from discussion the arbitration tribunals for disputes between companies and states makes me opposed to it. the united states and europe have powerful jurisdictional tools that make any isds system superfluous. priority must be given to strengthening european unity and to establishing economic and social governance to boost investment and employment. in a multipolar world, the european union must negotiate on an equal footing with the united states, but also with china, latin america and africa. i am for a humane europe in a fairer world. unfortunately, that is not the vision that was reflected in the resolution that is being proposed to us for adoption. it aims to indicate the 'red lines' of the ttip negotiations, but fails to protect all european standards.

in writing. ‒ fishing vessels flying the venezuelan flag have been allowed to operate in the exclusive economic zone of french guiana, an overseas department, for several decades. however, given the economic and social importance of these fishing activities, and given that the council and the commission considered it inappropriate to terminate them, a different practice was followed: access for venezuelan fishing vessels operating in european union waters off the coast of guyana was granted in the form of a council declaration which, in accordance with the case law of the international court of justice, produces legal effects in international law. the european parliament yesterday gave a favourable opinion in favour of this proposal being approved as soon as possible, which is now possible by resolving the institutional conflict, which had its sole source in a disagreement on the exact legal basis. this will allow fishing activities in the area concerned, the regularity of which has not been affected by this delay, to be covered by the appropriate legal framework.

in writing. ‒ intermodal travel, i.e. moving easily across borders using different modes of transport (train, tram, bus, etc.) is a concept we support. we are aware of the difficulties in that regard, including national ticketing websites with information available only in a foreign local language. however, the fact that the difficulties have to be solved by means of a single ticket or e-platform cannot be justified in terms of cost. the report is full of such unrealistic proposals (disproportionate liability of small carriers for missed connecting long-haul flights, advanced digital real-time systems in buses in rural areas...). however, we do believe that regional and national transport companies should bundle their timetables at national level and make them available as open data to companies working on integrated platforms. google maps, for example, shows the door-to-door route at a glance, including for cross-border public transport, as long as it has access to the journey timetables. the nva delegation therefore, in line with the position of its ecr group, merely abstained. this is a signal that the european commission should focus on non-legislative action to support the relevant sectors rather than to weaken them.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on draft amending budget no 1/2015 of the european union for the financial year 2015 in order to adopt the draft budget as presented by the commission and thus to implement the european fund for strategic investments as quickly as possible. i am pleased that agreement was reached quickly between all the institutions on this fund. since the 2008 financial crisis, both public and private investment has remained abnormally low in the european union. we therefore need a plan to boost investment to put europe back on the path to sustainable and inclusive growth. unfortunately, i must still deplore the redeployment from the connecting europe facility (cef) and horizon 2020. these programmes are of great importance for employment and growth. finally, i support the idea that investments in research and transport will help to boost growth, competitiveness and employment, and achieve the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy.
