in writing. ‒ i have mixed feelings when reading this report on the impact of mass migration on the eu budget. it is good to see that the rapporteur is aware of the seriousness of the situation and has the courage to write literally that migration can be costly. for years, it was politically unthinkable that this painful truth would ever be proclaimed. it is now important to act on this knowledge, and that is where the problem lies. this report emphasizes the importance of frontex and europol, which is progress in itself, but only if frontex is used to restrict immigration rather than facilitate it. this document goes far too far and does not touch the heart of the matter, namely that the whole schengen treaty should be revised and that member states should therefore be given the freedom to carry out targeted border controls again. the whole of the eu's migration policy has turned into a nightmare. the member states must therefore be able to respond ad rem to the influx of fortune seekers coming to our countries.
in writing. ‒ almost daily we hear of the tragedies of refugees in the mediterranean and of hundreds of deaths off the coast of lampedusa. it is time for the eu to provide the necessary means to prevent such tragedies in the long term. the eu is a strong defender of human rights. it should therefore do everything in its power to protect the lives of refugees and to prevent further tragedies. i therefore welcome the budgetary correction, even if further efforts will have to be made in the future.
in writing. ‒ this is a first step at budgetary level in relation to the issue of migration and the dramatic situation of migrants in the mediterranean. the increase of eur 75.7 million will allow the expansion of operations triton and poseidon, which are primarily intended to save lives at sea. i approved this proposal. however, even if these funds will increase the resources of europol, the european asylum support office and frontex, it is clear that these additional resources will be insufficient to cope with the magnitude of migratory trends, whether it is to save lives, to effectively combat traffickers or to scale up development and protection programmes for north africa.
in writing. ‒ by approving an additional €69.6 million for the budgets of frontex, europol and the european asylum support office, parliament is providing a first response to the most serious migration crisis europe has faced since the end of the second world war. the budget for operation triton (border surveillance) will be tripled from €2.9 million to €9 million per month, but europe will have to propose more concrete measures to stem this massive influx. it is necessary, in particular, to make frontex a genuine border protection agency, to develop a humanitarian visa system which does not force migrants to rely on criminal networks, and to establish a genuine community asylum policy.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report on draft amending budget no 5 to the 2015 budget which the european parliament approved on 7 july in strasbourg and which provides for measures to deal with migratory pressures. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the budget and will continue to monitor the implementation of the budget. an amount of eur 89 million in commitment appropriations and eur 76,6 million in payment appropriations is provided to finance the additional needs for migration measures. as part of these amounts can be financed through unused funds, the financial burden is actually eur 75,8 million in commitments and there is no need to provide for fresh money.
in writing. - i voted for it, of course. however, i am alarmed by the low amounts of the increases proposed in draft amending budget no 5/2015, which do not correspond to the real needs in view of the current crisis in the mediterranean which is likely to worsen further.
in writing. ‒ the milk quota scheme, which expired on 31 march 2015, presents major challenges for the european milk sector. the fluctuations in prices in particular are a serious problem for dairy farmers. i welcome this resolution, since it calls for regulatory instruments for crisis situations and for the strengthening of the market observatory.
in writing. ‒ the dairy sector was particularly affected by the end of milk quotas on 31 march and the impact of the russian embargo. this report, which i have approved, calls on the commission to implement a series of measures to counter these negative effects. it called on the commission to introduce new financing possibilities for the sector through eib aid, to revise intervention prices and to implement new regulatory measures to stabilise supply and prices paid to producers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the nicholson report, which is the european parliament's response to the commission's report on the evolution of the situation on the dairy market and the implementation of the 'milk package'. this is in the context of the end of the milk quota system since 31 march 2015. the new european approach is of course fraught with uncertainties and no one can predict whether its flagship measure, which is the possibility for farmers to collectively negotiate supply contracts with dairies, will be sufficient to guarantee a viable future for producers. in belgium, for example, this agreement is not mandatory and consists of a code of good practice signed by 98% of processors and the three main agricultural organisations. among the sensible proposals is the facility for farmers to join producer organisations (po) which can collectively negotiate the terms of contracts, including the price of raw milk. the negotiating power of milk producers is enhanced in a rather favourable environment, with the average price of milk in the european union rising to more than 40 ct/kg and consumer demand for milk products increasing.
in writing. ‒ the eu must ensure a better balance in the supply chain, introduce better tools against market disruption and help farmers find new outlets for their products, as called for by the european parliament in its adoption yesterday of a report on the milk and milk products sector. parliament called on the commission to intervene by introducing additional targeted market measures in the face of the crisis affecting national milk markets, as a result of the downward pressure on prices resulting from the lack of adequate crisis prevention instruments, a drop in world demand, global price volatility and the russian embargo. parliament regretted that the council had rejected its request for aid to producers who voluntarily reduced their production in the event of a serious crisis. parliament also called on the commission to implement more effective and realistic safety nets and to ensure that intervention prices (which are far too low) better reflect real production costs and real market prices and are better adapted to market changes.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament today took stock of the 'milk package', even though milk quotas have been abolished since 31 march. the socialist and radical meps have always opposed the end of milk quotas. for us, this was the system of public regulation of supply, which enabled both effective control of production, which was essential to maintain prices and incomes, and the maintenance of many family farms throughout the territory. unfortunately, during the cap reforms of 2003 and 2008, the right decided to liberalize the milk sector and put an end to milk quotas: since 31 march, nothing has stopped the movement towards geographical concentration of production in the territory. the most threatened are the small, medium-sized and isolated family farms.
in writing. ‒ this report calls on the commission to work towards ensuring that european companies have fair access to public procurement markets in third countries. the report particularly emphasises the involvement of european smes, which i welcome, as they are still the largest and most important employers in europe.
in writing. ‒ the report firstly recalls the importance of public-private partnerships (ppps) in economic development and job creation in the european union. however, it stresses the difficulties that european companies often encounter when participating in a ppp in a country outside the union. it therefore urged the commission to work, when negotiating trade and investment agreements with other countries, to remove the administrative, procedural and technical obstacles which prevent union companies, and smes in particular, from participating in ppps in third countries. i have approved this text, which is part of a desire to develop the union's enterprises and hence employment in a context of reciprocal trade with third countries.
philippe de backer (alde),in writing. – the eu is increasingly engaging with the private sector to promote growth and development in african countries. i support the need for better regulation on public-private partnerships, clear impact assessments and evaluation mechanisms. transparency and accountability are two very important concepts in this regard, and they need to be fully adhered to.
in writing. ‒ i voted this afternoon in favour of the zahradil report which stresses the importance of public-private partnerships (ppps) in developing countries. the plenary followed the recommendations of the committee on international trade, which advocated the development of ppps, drawing on european expertise in the field: the union dominates this market in the field of infrastructure, which accounts for more than 45% of the nominal value of ppps. the report highlights the positive experiences of ppps which have resulted in better project delivery, the possibility of financing long-term costs, and a more flexible and skilled management environment. the ppp has other advantages. at the heart of this partnership approach are the requirements of transparency and accountability, translated into english as 'accountability'. these are two requirements in today's economic world, marked by a reduction in public investment and a renewed approach to public management. this is a further reason for meps' support for the rise of public-private partnerships in developing countries, where they are often the only way to launch large-scale infrastructure projects.
in writing. - i voted for the text. recall the importance of public-private partnerships (ppps) as a driver of economic growth, innovation, competitiveness and job creation both within and outside the single market; it emphasises the strategic role of ppps in the modernisation of infrastructure, including energy, road, digital and water supply infrastructure. i would also like the commission to ensure that bodies supported by the european union, such as the european agency for small and medium-sized enterprises (easme) and the enterprise europe network (een), can also obtain and share with smes information on how to integrate ppps in third countries, and encourage the participation of small and medium-sized enterprises in ppps in third countries.
in writing. ‒ the melo report gives a good picture of the situation in the fruit and vegetables sector and touches on a number of pain points. the total eu support is steadily increasing, as is the degree of organisation in the sector with the creation and expansion of producer organisations . this does not prevent the steady decline in production area, the concentration of most of the subsidy pool in a limited number of pos and the low use of resources relating to crisis prevention and management, training and research and experimental production. the russian boycott is not the fault of the sector, but it is a big victim of it. the commission is leaning back, however.
in writing. ‒ fruit and vegetable production is under enormous pressure today. the strong concentration of retail and discount chains enables them to play an increasingly important role in setting market prices. producers are also facing increasing competition from third country products. the only way to solve our structural problems is to strengthen the role of our producer organizations. i welcome the report adopted, because it proposes, among other things, that we should form larger associations of producer organizations to strengthen the bargaining power of farmers in the food supply chain. it also points out that well-functioning producer organisations can be seen as an aspect of increasing the attractiveness of agriculture for young people, which could help to reverse the unsustainable demographic trend in this sector.
in writing. ‒ i have approved this report which draws attention to the difficulties faced by fruit and vegetable producers who are struggling to earn a decent living, in particular because of unfair commercial practices and pressure from large distribution groups, and therefore calls on the commission to step up efforts to combat these practices by establishing clear european rules. it also aims to make producer organisations more attractive by simplifying rules, promoting research and innovation and providing more funding to encourage more farmers to participate. finally, as the russian embargo on exports from the union has seriously affected many european producers, the report calls for the community support measures to be maintained in place as long as necessary until the normal market situation is fully restored.
in writing. ‒ everyone knows the importance of the health advice "eat 5 fruits and vegetables a day". unfortunately, this is not the case, as teenagers consume on average only 30 to 50% of the recommended daily allowance of fruit and vegetables, while 22 million children in the european union are overweight. this lack of fruit and vegetable intake can be the cause of many chronic diseases. it is also a direct problem for the fruit and vegetable sectors, with a loss of production in recent years, accentuated by the economic crisis marked by an increase in the consumption of processed foods and the russian embargo on many products: apples and pears, as in belgium. this is why the clear message of support for the european fruit and vegetable sector delivered this afternoon is so important. the european union must redouble its efforts to ensure the viability and sustainability of the sector. the objective of a fair income for farmers cannot be achieved without effective action against unfair trading practices in the food supply chain and policies aimed at greater protection and better outlets for producers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the fruit and vegetables sector since the 2007 reform for several reasons, firstly to ask the commission to set clear european standards to combat unfair practices and the pressure exerted by large-scale distribution on producers and their incomes, and secondly to ask for an increase in aid to producer organisations and the reintroduction of eu aid for investments by newly created organisations. i also ask the commission, by voting in favour of this report, to set up a mechanism for withdrawing products in the event of a crisis, in order to avoid serious losses for fruit and vegetable producers. finally, in this connection, i urge the commission to strengthen the aid schemes for the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk in schools. this will encourage young people to adopt a healthy, balanced diet.
in writing. - i voted for the report by mr melo. i believe that the commission should redouble its efforts to protect farmers from unfair trading practices by large retailers. it makes little sense to invest resources in strengthening and creating po (a slow and difficult process) if the bargaining power in the food chain continues to be predominantly retailer-owned. moreover, since many member states are adopting national measures to address these problems, some coordination is necessary at union level in order to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market. in any event, this issue will be dealt with more fully by the ep in a report to be prepared by our committee on the internal market and consumer protection (imco) in the coming weeks.
in writing. the european commission has announced that it will make the 2016 work programme a political document focusing on the main lines, the real priorities for 2016. that approach is a good one, at least if it sets the right priorities and is ambitious enough. and that may be where the shoe fits. the commission always says that the eu must be big in big things and small in small things. for me, this means that the eu must give priority to tackling the biggest problems, the problems facing eu citizens. this does not mean that social legislation is being abolished under the guise of reducing administrative burdens. problems that citizens are concerned about include social dumping, (youth) unemployment and tax evasion by multinationals. i therefore call on the commission to devote sufficient attention in the 2016 work programme to tackling these problems vigorously. the second report, on the implementation of the new rules, is to be submitted to the european parliament and the council by the end of the year. i hope that the commission will take this up in 2016 and not just study and evaluate it. the problems with the secondment directive are well known. it is time for action and solutions.
in writing. the implementation of this report will make a major step towards transparent operation of listed companies. this will be done without adding procedures or obligations which would place a burden on the undertakings concerned and without increasing their costs. this report is also consistent with our desire to reduce tax evasion and avoidance. the european parliament has indeed approved by a very large majority the principle of requiring multinational companies to file a country-by-country tax return which would fall within the public domain. the european union must play a leading role in drawing as many countries as possible into its wake. all available information and resources must be used to put an end to the massive tax evasion which is depriving the public authorities of substantial revenues at a time when citizens are being hit hard by austerity policies.

in writing. ‒ promoting free trade between eu countries, but also with the us, is a good thing. after all, economics does not have to be a zero-sum game where one party loses and the other party wins. it can be a win-win. but ttip is an example of backroom politics. a gigantic treaty is being negotiated above the heads of the citizens and the consequences are unknown. the european commission believes that ttip will benefit the european economy, but the commission's analyses often lack a time horizon and sound econometric models. the american tufts university is already forecasting a loss of 450,000 jobs in the european union, and it is not alone. academicians of the british royal economic society say of this: "ideology obscures reality", he said. apart from the arguments relating to public health, the environment, isds and transparency, it is already clear what lies ahead. at the micro level, small and mediumsized enterprises will be the losers of ttip. at the macro level, the northern member states in particular will suffer from the disadvantages of this agreement. as if the monetary union with its unprecedented north-south transfers were not enough!
in writing. ‒ after a thorough examination of the matter, i feel that my initial feeling that i cannot support ttip has been reinforced. first of all, i deeply regret that parliamentary control - one of the most important powers of this house - is being left out of the negotiations. the fact that we members are only given a limited and incomplete view of the negotiating texts is an unacceptable democratic deficit. i am also categorically opposed to the use of extraordinary investor-state dispute settlement (isds) procedures. indeed, there are no compelling reasons why an isds procedure between advanced judicial systems is necessary. that is why i have tabled an amendment explicitly rejecting the inclusion of isds in ttip. finally, i have economic concerns. the commission's study shows that the additional growth forecast of 0.5% is de facto a very optimistic scenario and will not have its full effect until 2027. until then, and counting down to a single year, we would have an average growth of only 0.041 percentage points per year. i have therefore voted against this resolution.
in writing. ‒ the ps's message was and will remain very clear: - no to the isds mechanism, because the european and american legal systems are perfectly equipped to ensure the protection of investments; - no to the privatisation of the public service. we demand the total and unconditional preservation of public services of general interest and reject the negative lists of liberalisation of services;-no to social and environmental standards which are neither ambitious nor binding;-no to regulatory cooperation, this mechanism which consists of making multinationals and other industrial lobbies a quasi-co-legislator and which leads to the lowering in the short, medium and long term of our european standards (social, environmental, food safety, etc.);-no to the abandonment of the precautionary principle, data protection or cultural diversity. despite all our amendments, they have not been respected, particularly with regard to isds. we therefore voted against and will remain extremely vigilant as to the outcome of the negotiations. our socialist delegation will be unyielding in any event and will reject any free trade agreement which could endanger the general interest of the european citizens.
in writing. ‒ the eu and the us are the world's largest trading partners, trading €2 billion of goods and services each day. the trade and investment agreement is designed to stimulate growth and jobs. we call for a balanced agreement respecting the highest social, environmental and health standards. that is a basic condition for us. the main guideline is that companies on both sides can fight with the same weapons, and that we make sure that certain standards that are important to us are not affected. parliament must have the last word on what it can and cannot do. the commission has therefore proposed that the member states should establish a clear list of services which can compete in each other's markets, excluding services of general interest such as education and health care. we also send a clear signal to the negotiators: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. such a mechanism can only be provided that democracy is not compromised and that it is a step towards an international arbitration court in due course. we now expect the european commission, which is negotiating on behalf of europe, to follow up on our recommendations. we'll be watching that closely.

in writing. ‒ this report will make a major step towards transparent operation of listed companies. this will be done without adding any procedures or obligations which would increase the burden on the undertakings concerned or their costs. this report is also consistent with our desire to reduce tax evasion and avoidance. the european union must play a leading role in drawing as many countries as possible into its wake.
in writing. – i voted in favour of this report as it represents a strong compromise between the main groups of the european parliament. more importantly, the report avoids the tsunami of unnecessarily detailed regulations which was initially being proposed by the socialist rapporteur. europe needs simplified rules and a common market that functions more effectively than today. we need to provide business owners and entrepreneurs the possibility to use more of their time on running and developing their businesses, rather than dealing with bureaucracy. i believe this report is important if europe is to address the roots of the financial crisis and corporate governance shortcomings. the report aims to contribute to long-term shareholder engagement. it calls for more transparency on internal business transactions which could possibly jeopardise the company, but protecting at the same time business sensitive information. i specifically welcome the flexibility clauses of the text and the comply or explain approach, leaving enough leeway for the management boards of companies.
in writing. ‒ i strongly supported the compromise that led to this resolution because it aims to increase transparency and encourage long-term shareholder commitment to companies. this text puts an end to the disparity of legislation which has existed up to now. at present, 13 member states allow shareholders to have a say on remuneration policy. fifteen eu countries communicate on remuneration policy and eleven require the publication of directors' remuneration on an individual basis. europe needs simplified, harmonised and transparent rules, which should help to steer businesses and investors towards long-term decision-making and will also make it possible to combat tax evasion and fraud more effectively. in addition, by requiring large and listed companies to publish country-by-country information on revenues, taxes paid on profits and subsidies received, the text should help to address some of the shortcomings in corporate governance and address the root causes of the financial crisis.
in writing. ‒ after long and bitter negotiations between the political groups and thanks to the compromise reached, the european parliament supported the cofferati report encouraging the long-term involvement of shareholders in the project of listed companies, rather than speculation. the financial crisis has exposed certain corporate governance deficiencies in listed companies, including insufficient long-term shareholder commitment and a lack of transparency. thanks to the fight of my political group, the alliance of liberals and democrats for europe, the compromise text adopted today strikes the right balance between full transparency where there is a real benefit to shareholders and other stakeholders, and the protection of sensitive information of companies, while guaranteeing sufficient room for manoeuvre to the boards of directors of companies. for the single market to work better, europe needs simplified rules. we must provide the opportunity for employers and entrepreneurs to devote more of their time to running and developing their businesses, rather than to bureaucracy. the text adopted by meps this afternoon goes in that direction.
in writing. ‒ at its july plenary, the european parliament voted in favour of a country-by-country tax return for multinationals. i fully supported this measure which aims to oblige multinational companies to be more transparent in their taxation vis-à-vis the general public. two elements seem particularly important to me: 1) parliament requires large companies to publish once a year a report detailing the following information country by country: list and purpose of all legal entities owned by them, number of employees, turnover, profit (or loss) before tax, taxes paid, public subsidies received; 2) parliament also requires these large companies to provide once a year the essential elements and information of tax returns (which has been much discussed following the luxleaks case), again on a country-by-country basis. it is now up to the council of the european union to take a position, but it cannot ignore a proposal voted by such a large majority (556 for, 67 against and 87 abstentions).
in writing. - i voted for it. at present, too many companies are overly focused on satisfying demands for high short-term profits and returns. in order to solve, at least partially, these problems, we wanted to give minority shareholders, and in particular institutional investors, a more transparent, manageable and influential role in corporate governance. the idea is that if investors are more committed and more long-term oriented in their commitment, companies will give higher priority to long-term concerns. this new focus will in turn benefit the end-consumers of institutional investors and asset managers, businesses and society as a whole.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the establishment and use of a market stability reserve for the eu greenhouse gas emission allowance trading scheme. the commission has also received comments from the united kingdom, the united kingdom and the united states on the application of the measures. this surplus is estimated at 2 billion. this has not been able to create a strong incentive for investment in low-emission technologies.
in writing. ‒ the rapporteur supports the commission's proposal to create a market stability reserve, as this is a structural reform which will introduce rules in the ets directive to govern market fluctuations and in particular the supply of allowances. the council stressed in october 2014 that this would be the main instrument to achieve the greenhouse gas emission reduction target. i approved this report.
in writing. – i voted in favour of the market stability reserve compromise because i believe the ets system did not deliver what it was expected to do. carbon prices are too low and do not offer a sufficient incentive for companies to invest in more carbon-efficient techniques. at the same time we have to prevent carbon leakage by safeguarding companies that are price takers on the global markets from additional costs. the innovation fund should also support companies in making the move to more carbon-efficient technologies.
in writing. ‒ i supported this afternoon the report by ivo belet on the creation and operation of a market stability reserve for the eu's greenhouse gas emission allowance trading system. behind this barbaric headline is a matter of the utmost importance: the use of a market instrument to reduce co2 emissions. and there is a lot to be done, partly because the carbon market is not working well, tainted by the mistakes of the beginning: surplus free allocation of carbon quotas and the inability to stabilize the price of carbon so that it is an incentive to invest in clean technologies. in view of this, it was essential that the european parliament support the commission's proposal to create a market stability reserve, in particular by playing on the supply of allowances, and by setting aside 900 million emission allowances. this is a good way to clean up the market, to tackle the problem of the surplus of allowances, currently estimated at over 2 billion, and thus to maintain the course the union has set itself: a 40% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030.
in writing. ‒ the vote in parliament on wednesday will pave the way for structural reform of the eu emissions trading system (ets) by creating an operational market stability reserve as of 1 january 2019. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the context of the directive on the protection of the environment. this is therefore a first step towards the longer-term reform of the ets that the european commission is preparing for the post-2020 period (fourth ets trading period) with a proposal expected on 15 july. the ball is now in the court of the eu council, which will formally adopt the text (amending directive 2003/87/ec) next september.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the text of my colleague ivo belet. an efficient and reformed emissions trading system (ets) with a market stabilisation tool, as proposed by the commission, will be the main instrument of the european union to achieve this greenhouse gas emission reduction target, as indicated in the conclusions of the european council of 23 october 2014.
in writing. ‒ the proposal for a directive put to the vote puts an end to the possibility of excluding seafarers from the application of certain directives relating to labour law (information and consultation of workers, collective redundancies, european works councils, etc.). i voted in favour of this proposal.
in writing. the fisheries sector is a major employer in europe. the most recent figures show that almost 150 000 jobs have been created. these encouraging prospects should not make us forget the need to ensure safe and fair working conditions for all europeans, including seafarers. the aim of the directive is to improve living and working conditions on board vessels and to exploit the potential of innovation in the maritime sector in order to make it more attractive, particularly for young people who are hard hit by unemployment. i therefore support this report.
in writing. ‒ this afternoon, the european parliament supported, by a very large majority (642 votes in favour, 38 against and 24 abstentions), the morin-chartier report amending five directives on workers' rights, in order to improve the protection of seafarers in eu labour legislation. in general, eu labour law applies to workers in all sectors. however, today there are several directives which allow member states to exclude seafarers from certain provisions relating to the protection of workers. this inevitably leads to unequal treatment of these workers across europe and has repercussions on competition in the shipping and fisheries sectors. the aim of this directive is to align the rights of workers in the sector with those of workers on land in terms of equal pay for equal work, without distinction of nationality, place of residence, race, sex, sexual orientation, disability or age. the proposal also aims to increase the number of jobs in the maritime sector and to make working conditions more attractive to encourage young europeans to take up a maritime career at a time when the sector is experiencing a real decline.
in writing. ‒ it was abnormal that workers in the maritime sector, better known as 'seafarers', were excluded or could be excluded from the scope of several european directives on labour law. i am particularly pleased that the commission has taken this initiative. i therefore voted in favour of the report by my colleague, mrs elisabeth morin-chartier, which is in line with the european commission's legislative proposal to improve the working conditions of these people. we must put an end to the exclusionary possibilities which penalise seafarers in relation to a significant part of european labour law. the report was adopted by a large majority, with 624 meps voting in favour of the text (38 against and 24 abstentions). this result shows the injustice experienced by workers in the maritime sector in recent years.
in writing. ‒ the european commission's proposal aims to improve the working conditions of seafarers working on board ships flying the flag of one of the 28 eu member states, while taking into account the specificities of this sector of activity. the proposal for a directive therefore revises five previously adopted directives which excluded seafarers from their scope. the european commission wanted to point out that the exclusions for seafarers in these five directives were not part of the commission's initial proposals, but were the result of negotiations with the other partners. i share the rapporteur's view and therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ since the crisis, many people have been unemployed. youth unemployment in the eu is over 20%. european solutions are needed to solve this problem in the long term. these guidelines for employment policy are also reflected in the europe 2020 strategy. employment policy is listed as one of the priorities for further boosting eu growth and overcoming the consequences of the crisis once and for all. that is why i support the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, which contains several positive recommendations, namely:- the creation of sustainable and quality jobs for all (socio-economic security, adequate wages, decent working conditions, social protection, gender equality, vocational training, etc.); - convergence of working conditions through the top; - the fight against poverty, etc. these are the priorities which must guide the union's policies if we are to get out of the blind austerity and regain the confidence of the citizens.
in writing. the treaty on the functioning of the european union provides that member states are to regard economic policies and the promotion of employment as matters of common concern and to coordinate their action within the council. access to meaningful employment for all citizens of the union is a prerequisite not only for their individual fulfilment but also for the return of smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. as a federalist, i am deeply convinced that closer cooperation between the member states in an increasing number of areas will help to revive a europe which is still too often the sum of its national interests.
in writing. today, parliament gave its consent to a council decision on guidelines for member states' employment policies in 2015. the eight guidelines proposed by the commission include stimulating investment, removing obstacles to employment and stimulating demand and improving the supply of jobs. emphasis is also placed on combating poverty and promoting equal opportunities. member states are called upon to ensure better access for women to the labour market, to promote entrepreneurship among young people and to combat discrimination in the labour market, in particular discrimination against people with disabilities or older workers. the text also stresses the importance of education and the prevention of early school leaving, as well as adult training programmes. improving the match between demand and supply of jobs is crucial to optimise the functioning of the labour market. employment, the fight against poverty and education are politically intrinsically linked issues which must be considered and implemented together.
in writing. ‒ every year at the same time, since 2005, the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states are proposed by the commission and approved by the council. 2015 is no exception and each capital received an opinion presenting an overview of national employment policies and the common objectives to be achieved. some member states, such as belgium under the government of charles michel, are doing well, a trend confirmed by the oecd which stated in its oecd360 report that "belgium is doing well, particularly with a gross domestic product above the average, which is important for well-being". other member states, not just greece, are struggling to initiate the structural reforms needed to boost growth and reduce unemployment: nearly 24 million people were unemployed in the union in january 2015, including 18 million in the euro area alone. it is unworthy of european society. all efforts in the years ahead must be directed towards one single objective: the access or return to employment of citizens of working age.
in writing. ‒ the employment guidelines were first adopted in 2010 to support the europe 2020 strategy. while these guidelines remained stable between 2010 and 2014, the commission proposed a set of new guidelines for member states' employment policies for 2015. these new guidelines should contribute to achieving smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. the european parliament, in voting in favour of the report on the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states, calls on the european union to support the creation of quality jobs. as a supporter of a socially regulated market economy, i advocate a reduction in precarious employment, underemployment, undeclared work and zero-hour contracts. in this report, the european parliament also recommends that member states, in accordance with national practice, implement a minimum wage commensurate with the socioeconomic situation of the country. this is a possible measure to combat poverty. that is one of the reasons why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the amendments tabled by our colleague the rapporteur on this matter. particular efforts should be made to increase the employment of workers with very low levels of education or qualifications and those who are not able to acquire training or skills quickly, and to reduce large-scale and long-term unemployment, which is steadily increasing, with particular attention to regions lagging behind.

in writing. ‒ globalisation is inevitable and goes hand in hand with the opening up of new markets, international competition, economic growth and job creation. the downside of this is job losses in less competitive sectors. the nva delegation in the european parliament understands the objectives of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf), but also has an eye on the taxpayer who pays the bill. moreover, social policy should be a competence of the member states in the first instance. a european transfer union is not a panacea for tackling unemployment. in particular, structural reforms are needed to get back on track with economic growth. the n-va meps therefore abstained on this dossier.
in writing. ‒ the redundancies will only worsen the unemployment situation in the region of northern ostrobothnia (part of the nuts level fi1a region), where 424 of the 568 redundancies took place. the unemployment rate in this region is still a few percentage points above the national average. we have shown our solidarity and voted in favour of the request.
